![Quickstart demo: Aspire dashboard showing services running, a command sent via Swagger UI, and the resulting event in the event stream](docs/assets/quickstart-demo.gif) # Hexalith.EventStore — DAPR-native event sourcing server for .NET [![GitHub stars](https://img.shields.io/github/stars/Hexalith/Hexalith.EventStore)](https://github.com/Hexalith/Hexalith.EventStore/stargazers) [![NuGet](https://img.shields.io/nuget/v/Hexalith.EventStore.Contracts)](https://www.nuget.org/packages/Hexalith.EventStore.Contracts) [![Build](https://img.shields.io/github/actions/workflow/status/Hexalith/Hexalith.EventStore/ci.yml?branch=main)](https://github.com/Hexalith/Hexalith.EventStore/actions/workflows/ci.yml) [![Docs](https://img.shields.io/github/actions/workflow/status/Hexalith/Hexalith.EventStore/docs-validation.yml?branch=main&label=Docs)](https://github.com/Hexalith/Hexalith.EventStore/actions/workflows/docs-validation.yml) [![License: MIT](https://img.shields.io/badge/License-MIT-yellow.svg)](LICENSE) If you've spent weeks wiring up an event store, a message broker, multi-tenant isolation, and a read-model refresh story — only to realize you'll do it again for your next project — we built this for you. Hexalith.EventStore is a distributed, CQRS and DDD-ready event sourcing framework that handles command routing, event persistence, snapshots, query execution, and pub/sub delivery so you can focus on domain logic. Built on DAPR for infrastructure portability. ## The Programming Model Your domain logic lives in an aggregate class with typed `Handle` methods — conceptually a pure function: $(Command, CurrentState?) \rightarrow List$. Each `Handle` method receives a specific command and the current state, then returns a `DomainResult` carrying success events or rejections. ```csharp public sealed class CounterAggregate : EventStoreAggregate { public static DomainResult Handle(IncrementCounter command, CounterState? state) => DomainResult.Success(new IEventPayload[] { new CounterIncremented() }); public static DomainResult Handle(DecrementCounter command, CounterState? state) { if ((state?.Count ?? 0) == 0) return DomainResult.Rejection(new IRejectionEvent[] { new CounterCannotGoNegative() }); return DomainResult.Success(new IEventPayload[] { new CounterDecremented() }); } public static DomainResult Handle(ResetCounter command, CounterState? state) { if ((state?.Count ?? 0) == 0) return DomainResult.NoOp(); return DomainResult.Success(new IEventPayload[] { new CounterReset() }); } } public sealed class CounterState { public int Count { get; private set; } public void Apply(CounterIncremented e) => Count++; public void Apply(CounterDecremented e) => Count--; public void Apply(CounterReset e) => Count = 0; } ``` > Under the hood, `EventStoreAggregate` implements `IDomainProcessor` — you can still use that interface directly for advanced scenarios (see the legacy [`CounterProcessor`](samples/Hexalith.EventStore.Sample/Counter/CounterProcessor.cs) example). ## Why Hexalith? | Feature | Hexalith | Marten | EventStoreDB | Custom | | -------------------------- | -------------------------------- | -------------------- | --------------------------- | ------------ | | Infrastructure portability | Any store/broker, zero-code swap | PostgreSQL only | Dedicated server | You build it | | Multi-tenant isolation | Built-in: data, topics, access | Manual | Manual | You build it | | CQRS/ES framework | Complete, infra-agnostic | Complete, PG-coupled | Storage only, BYO framework | You build it | | Deployment | DAPR sidecar: Docker, K8s, ACA | App library | Server + clients | You build it | | Database lock-in | None (Redis, PG, Cosmos, etc.) | PostgreSQL | EventStoreDB | Chosen DB | > **Note:** Hexalith is not the right tool for every scenario. If you need raw event stream performance or already run PostgreSQL everywhere, see the [decision aid](docs/concepts/choose-the-right-tool.md). ## Get Started Register the event store in two lines — `AddEventStore()` scans your assembly for aggregate types, no manual registration needed: ```csharp builder.Services.AddEventStore(); // Auto-discovers CounterAggregate // ... app.UseEventStore(); // Activates domains with convention-derived names ``` Beyond commands, the platform includes a query pipeline with ETag-based cache validation, projection invalidation hooks, preflight authorization endpoints, and optional SignalR notifications for real-time read-model refresh. **Get started in under 10 minutes** — follow the [Quickstart Guide](docs/getting-started/quickstart.md). Prerequisites: [.NET SDK 11.0.100](https://dotnet.microsoft.com/download/dotnet/11.0) (as pinned in `global.json`) and the [.NET 11 runtime](https://dotnet.microsoft.com/download/dotnet/11.0), [Docker Desktop](https://www.docker.com/products/docker-desktop/), [DAPR CLI](https://docs.dapr.io/getting-started/install-dapr-cli/) ## Run and Debug in the Platform Workspace EventStore runs and debugs as a module from the [Hexalith.Platform](https://github.com/Hexalith/Hexalith.Platform) workspace, where this repository is the `references/Hexalith.EventStore` submodule. If NuGet uses a custom `globalPackagesFolder`, set `NUGET_PACKAGES` to that absolute folder for both restore and `debug`; otherwise the tool checks `~/.nuget/packages` and reports `HXR016` if the packages are missing. `debug` builds `references/Hexalith.EventStore` in Debug, starts the declared module within Platform's selected development topology, waits for `/ready`, and reports the `dotnet run` launcher process id. Attach your debugger to the launcher's child process (`ps --ppid -o pid,args`). Stay attached until you finish, then stop the run with `down`. See [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md#run-and-debug-in-the-platform-workspace) and the Platform README for the full prerequisites. `debug` does not print the run id: it is the file name of the run state `.json` under `${XDG_DATA_HOME:-$HOME/.local/share}/hexalith-builds/g4-runs/` on Linux. Inspect the state files and select the one whose `projectProcessIds` contains the launcher id reported by this `debug` invocation. Confirm its `manifestHash` matches `sha256sum references/Hexalith.EventStore/module/hexalith.module-manifest.v2.json` (ignoring hexadecimal letter case), then use its `runId`. File modification time alone cannot identify your run. When an earlier run used the same manifest, `down --manifest` refuses with `HXR024`; add `--run-id `. An explicit `--run-id` is not cross-checked against the manifest, so verify both fields before stopping it. This repository's own `src/Hexalith.EventStore.AppHost` serves only this repository's own tests. A run of it is never evidence that EventStore runs in the Platform composition. ## Architecture ```mermaid flowchart TB Client([Client Application]) -->|REST commands + queries| CommandAPI[Command API Gateway] Realtime[Realtime UI / Client] <-.->|SignalR change notifications| CommandAPI CommandAPI -->|Route command| Actor[Aggregate Actor] Actor -->|Invoke| Domain[Domain Service
IDomainProcessor] Domain -->|Return events| Actor Actor -->|Persist| StateStore[(State Store
Redis / PostgreSQL / Cosmos DB)] Actor -->|Publish| PubSub{{Pub/Sub
RabbitMQ / Kafka / Azure Service Bus}} PubSub -->|Subscribe| Projections[Event Handlers / Projections] Projections -->|Projection changed| CommandAPI subgraph DAPR ["DAPR Sidecar (Infrastructure Abstraction)"] StateStore PubSub end ```
Architecture diagram text description The system follows a command-event architecture with a built-in read-model refresh path: client applications send commands and queries via REST to the Command API Gateway, which routes commands to Aggregate Actors and queries to projection handlers. Each actor invokes the domain service (your `IDomainProcessor` implementation) and persists resulting events to a state store. Events are published to a pub/sub system for downstream consumers, and projection changes can be surfaced back to clients through HTTP cache validators and optional SignalR notifications. DAPR provides the infrastructure abstraction layer, allowing you to swap state stores (Redis, PostgreSQL, Cosmos DB) and message brokers (RabbitMQ, Kafka, Azure Service Bus) without changing application code.

After all handlers prepare successfully, the dispatcher persists these through `ReadModelGenerationStaging` in resumable groups below the normal batch limits, then coordinates only the canonical authority operations. It preserves Prepared work, including guarded rebuilds, and never uses erasure retirement for ordinary delivery recovery. Discoverable enrollment performs this settlement before adding another active registration. Both store profiles retain matching participant counts, terminal fences and content-free manifest barriers; all discoverable batches obey the hard recovery limits even when guarded ownership permits `RetainManifestForRecovery=false`.

# Hexalith.Parties

Hexalith.Parties is a ready-to-deploy party management domain service for people and organizations. Public command and query traffic goes through Hexalith.EventStore; the `parties` service runs an EventStore SDK domain-service host behind that gateway, and consumers normally use the typed .NET client package. The solution also includes `parties-ui`, a Blazor Server browser UI/BFF for the Admin and Consumer experiences.

> **GDPR Notice:** Some GDPR infrastructure exists, and crypto-shredding is enabled by default, but the default key store is `LocalDevKeyStorageBackend` (in-memory, dev-only). **Do not store regulated EU personal data** until a production KMS or secret-store-backed key provider is provisioned. The MVP warning switch is separate from the crypto feature; see [deployment-guide.md](docs/deployment-guide.md) for the current runtime ownership boundary.

## Consuming the Parties Aspire helper

`Hexalith.Parties.Aspire` adds the separately built Parties server to a consuming
AppHost with `AddHexalithPartiesServer(eventStore, daprConfigPath)`. It delegates
state-store, pub/sub, health and sidecar wiring to `Hexalith.EventStore.Aspire`;
the package does not depend on the Parties server. The consumer supplies
Gateway routing, JWT validation and the app-channel token through platform helpers.
Source is resolved only in the owning repository or its direct
`references/Hexalith.Parties` checkout, and must be built before launch.
The helper is included in the normal protected release; adding source does not
mean a version is published or approved for downstream enrollment.

## Key Features

- **EventStore gateway** -- Public command/query ingress uses `POST /api/v1/commands` and `POST /api/v1/queries` with `Domain="party"`.
- **Parties domain-service host** -- The `parties` resource owns domain execution and SDK projection/query handlers behind EventStore.
- **Typed client package** -- `IPartiesCommandClient` and `IPartiesQueryClient` hide EventStore envelope plumbing for .NET consumers.
- **Parties UI/BFF** -- `parties-ui` is a Blazor Server host with FrontComposer, FluentUI, host-owned OIDC, role-gated Admin/Consumer areas, accessibility gates, and server-side token handling.
- **Admin portal RCL** -- `Hexalith.Parties.AdminPortal` provides the protected `/admin/parties*` browse/detail/create/edit/GDPR surfaces embedded by `parties-ui`.
- **Consumer portal RCL** -- `Hexalith.Parties.ConsumerPortal` provides the protected `/me*` Consumer profile, consent, data export, erasure, and processing-transparency surfaces embedded by `parties-ui`.
- **Embeddable party picker** -- `Hexalith.Parties.Picker` provides a Blazor/custom-element selector that searches through `IPartiesQueryClient` and emits durable party-id selections.
- **Separate MCP host** -- `parties-mcp` exposes `create_party`, `get_party`, `find_parties`, `update_party`, and `delete_party` through the typed client boundary.
- **DAPR event subscription** -- Subscriber apps consume EventStore-published party events with their own idempotent handlers.
- **EventStore Admin UI** -- Use `eventstore-admin-ui` for generic stream and event browsing.
- **.NET Aspire** -- One-command local topology with EventStore, Parties, Parties UI, Tenants, DAPR sidecars, Redis, and optional Keycloak.

## Quick Start

Set `HEXALITH_DAPR_HOME` to a prepared, absolute isolated Dapr home before
starting. Follow the [pinned Platform v1.7.1 runtime prerequisites](https://github.com/Hexalith/Hexalith.Platform/blob/0f4e27f1f78310bd731c10c19dc51bb1e0345d44/README.md#run-and-debug-a-technical-module);
the tool refuses an unset or unprepared home.

```bash
git clone https://github.com/Hexalith/Hexalith.Parties.git
cd Hexalith.Parties
git submodule update --init references/Hexalith.Platform references/Hexalith.Builds references/Hexalith.Commons references/Hexalith.EventStore references/Hexalith.FrontComposer references/Hexalith.PolymorphicSerializations references/Hexalith.Tenants references/Hexalith.Memories references/Hexalith.McpCli
dotnet tool restore
dotnet tool run hexalith-module -- debug --manifest module/hexalith.module-manifest.v2.json
```

The repository pins module tool **4.48.0** alongside aspirate and uses Aspire CLI
**13.6.5**. From this independent checkout, `debug` resolves direct references
once, builds the selected
source projects in Debug, and waits for exactly `parties`, `eventstore`, `tenants`,
`tenants-api`, `memories`, `memories-access-telemetry-clock`, and `memories-access-telemetry`.
The tool reports its run ID and source mapping; attach the debugger to the Parties
service child process. Stop that exact environment with
`dotnet tool run hexalith-module -- down --manifest module/hexalith.module-manifest.v2.json --run-id <run-id>`.
Initialize only this checkout's direct references; leave their nested references
uninitialized. Ordinary package CI keeps package references and Release builds.

Source preparation on 2026-10-31 succeeds with module tool 4.39.0 after
synchronizing the committed Platform identity. The tool derives its catalog
from the parent repository's committed Platform gitlink, then that Platform
commit's Builds gitlink. Stage selected source checkouts consistently and commit
the Platform selection before retrying a stale-catalog diagnostic. Runtime
topology qualification remains separate from successful build preparation.

The owner ACL remains `src/Hexalith.Parties.AppHost/DaprComponents/accesscontrol.parties.yaml`.
The renderer derives only `callers` and `invocationRules` from that ACL; its
`TEMPLATE` in `scripts/render-platform-declaration.py` owns all other declaration
fields. The strict parser accepts exactly thirteen unique POST routes from
EventStore with the existing deny defaults, trust domain and namespace. After an
owner-approved ACL change, run `python3 scripts/render-platform-declaration.py`;
adding or removing routes also requires an approved update to the parser's
thirteen-route invariant and its tests. Change `TEMPLATE` for non-ACL declaration
updates, then regenerate. CI requires
`python3 scripts/render-platform-declaration.py --check` and validates the generated
declaration with its reference declarations using the pinned tool.
Platform binds security storage through `Parties:Security:StateStoreName` and the
existing projection/mapping component keys. The declarative tenant subscription
uses `system.tenants.events` at `/tenants/events`; rich Memories search stays disabled.

**Legacy hosting scope:** `Hexalith.Parties.AppHost`, Aspire helpers, UI, proprietary
MCP and sample hosts remain for existing owner tests and continuity. They are frozen
and are outside this Platform qualification. The legacy local command is
`aspire run --apphost src/Hexalith.Parties.AppHost`; its Keycloak, admin and
UI topology is separate from the seven-server minimum above. Retirement requires
owner-approved parity and consumer-removal gates.

> **Prerequisite - tenant access state.** Provision or use an active Hexalith.Tenants tenant membership before the first Parties call. EventStore owns public authentication, tenant validation, RBAC, command/query routing, and generic response mapping. Parties consumes the authorized command/query behind the domain-service host and does not manage tenant lifecycle or roles itself.

The internal DAPR access-control policy is deny-by-default and permits only the
`eventstore` app ID to invoke the SDK domain routes: `/process`, `/query`,
`/admin/operational-index-metadata`, `/project`, `/project/v2`,
`/project/v2/reconcile`, `/replay-state`, `/project/rebuild/v1`,
`/project/rebuild/shared/v1`, `/project/rebuild/stage/v1`,
`/project/rebuild/commit/v1`, `/project/rebuild/abort/v1`, and
`/project/rebuild/verify/v1`. One documented exception: `accesscontrol.eventstore-admin.yaml`
is `defaultAction: allow` at the top level, because local self-hosted DAPR does
not reliably expose caller identity without mTLS (see
[`docs/event-publishing.md`](docs/event-publishing.md) for the full rationale).
Runtime deployment orchestration is externally
owned; the external orchestrator owns manifests, environment secrets, ingress,
promotion, and rollback. This repository publishes immutable workload images
and retains only local AppHost wiring.

See the [Getting Started Guide](docs/getting-started.md) for the full EventStore-fronted walkthrough.

### Generic McpCli command declarations (local migration increment)

The Contracts assembly declares exactly `parties.create-party`,
`parties.update-party`, `parties.reactivate-party` and `parties.deactivate-party`.
The module uses String identifiers, domain `party`, the existing full CLR command
wire names, and root `PartyId` for aggregate routing. Tenant authority remains in
the gateway envelope. `Hexalith.McpCli.Abstractions` 1.0.0 supplies declaration
attributes only; the package/source pair follows `UseHexalithProjectReferences`.
This increment does not enroll or publish a module or retire the legacy host.

McpCli payloads use exact CLR property casing and typed nested values. For example,
`parties.create-party` accepts:

```json
{"PartyId":"party-49","Type":"Person","PersonDetails":{"FirstName":"Ada","LastName":"Lovelace"},"ContactChannels":[{"PartyId":"party-49","ContactChannelId":"email-49","Type":"Email","Value":"ada@example.test","IsPreferred":true}]}
```

Supply IDs explicitly; every child `PartyId` must equal the root. No alias mapping,
ID generation, person/organization inference or read/merge patch is performed.
McpCli PartyId values use ASCII letters or digits plus `.`, `_` or `-`, start
and end with an ASCII letter or digit, and contain at most 128 characters.
McpCli refuses legacy braced, parenthesized and X-format GUID PartyId values
before Gateway submission, although Parties accepts them. Preserving those
legacy IDs or approving a conversion remains a C07 retirement gate.
An update supplies complete `PersonDetails` or `OrganizationDetails` replacements
and/or typed add, update or removal lists. A `PartyId`-only update is rejected;
every `UpdateContactChannels` item must supply at least one of `Type`, `Value` or
`IsPreferred` (including `false`). Activation is a separate command. Repeated
soft deactivation is a safe no-op after lifecycle guards and never performs GDPR
erasure.

Both shared composite validators enforce a maximum **raw UTF-16 length of 512
per string and 4096 combined**, without trimming or rewriting values. Every root,
nested, child and removal string occurrence counts, including whitespace and
repeated IDs. The tighter support-safe 128-character rule applies to `PartyId`,
`ContactChannelId`, `IdentifierId` and removal ID entries. Business identifier
`Value` strings retain the 512 UTF-16-unit limit. This is stricter than legacy wrapper counting of trimmed fields; the total
budget can bind before the configured composite sub-operation cap (default 100).
Explicit null lists and null list items reject; omitted lists retain empty defaults.
Create counts 1 plus every item in `ContactChannels` and `Identifiers` toward
the operation cap. Update counts each non-null details object plus every item
in its five operation lists. Removing a channel ID also listed for addition or
update rejects the entire update; adding and removing the same identifier ID
also rejects. An existing channel ID listed for both addition and update has
its addition skipped and its update applied.
All these checks run before protected aggregate state is accessed.

The four local vectors in `tests/conformance-vectors/mcpcli-v1/` target only the
unpublished scratch package `Hexalith.Parties.Contracts` **0.0.0-story49**. They
include prerequisite writes, repeat deactivation and semantic `parties.get-party`
postconditions using the approved `PartyDetail` / `party-detail` /
`PartyDetailProjectionQueryActor` route. Those Query contracts do not exist in this
increment: postconditions remain unexecuted until Story 4.10, which must rebind
vectors to the complete immutable artifact. Shared-validator format and artifact
checks do not prove handler effects. Stories 4.11/4.13 own parity and persistent
semantic proof. Maintainer approval must name the exact artifact hash and shared
validator revision. C06 error privacy, C07 legacy-ID reachability and C08 credential
and cross-tenant authorization evidence remain replacement/retirement gates.

The detail kind on update must match the existing party type; an update cannot
change that type. Omitted/null details preserve the existing object, while a
supplied object replaces it completely. Create requires the detail kind matching
`Type`, but also accepts/stores an extra opposite-kind object without changing
`Type`. Business identifiers are added or removed; there is no identifier-update
list. Contact updates require at least one non-null mutable member: omitted/null
preserves that member, `IsPreferred: false` clears that channel's preference,
and `Value: ""` replaces the value with an empty string. All contact kinds,
including PostalAddress/SocialMedia, store a raw string; no structured format is
defined. Preference is scoped to channel type; supply `IsPreferred: true` with a
type change to reconcile preferences in the target type.

`OrganizationDetails.IsNaturalPerson` defaults to false and initializes party
classification on create. Existing detail replacement changes the nested flag
without updating the established party classification; these four operations do
not provide a classification-change command. Lifecycle operations require an
existing unrestricted party with current erasure status Active, including
when requesting an already-current active state.

### Generic McpCli read declarations (local candidate)

The Contracts candidate declares exactly seven operations: `parties.get-party`,
`parties.list-parties`, `parties.search-parties`, `parties.create-party`,
`parties.update-party`, `parties.reactivate-party` and `parties.deactivate-party`.
The complete candidate still requires fresh maintainer approval, exact-source CI,

pinned in Builds and enrolled in McpCli. The existing five-tool MCP host remains
available; this declaration work does not authorize retirement.

Queries use domain `party` and envelope tenant authority. Detail uses wire type
`PartyDetail`, projection `party-detail`, historical compatibility name
`PartyDetailProjectionQueryActor`, and root `PartyId`. List and search use wire
`PartyIndex` / `PartySearch`, projection `party-index`, compatibility name
`PartyIndexProjectionQueryActor`, and aggregate `parties`. The current SDK
`PartyDetailQueryHandler`, `PartyIndexQueryHandler` and `PartySearchQueryHandler`
dispatch directly to canonical read models; actor compatibility fields do not
prove actor execution. Omitted EntityId falls back to AggregateId; supplied
EntityId must match before any read. String IDs retain existing Parties syntax;
McpCli still refuses legacy braced, parenthesized and X-format GUID IDs.

Erased detail has the same safe not-found outcome as missing detail. Inactive
detail stays visible. List accepts optional `Type` (Person or Organization),
`Active`, and inclusive `CreatedAfter`, `CreatedBefore`, `ModifiedAfter` and
`ModifiedBefore` instants with explicit offsets. Invalid instants and inverted
ranges reject. Search accepts `Query`, `Type` and `Active`; it trims the query
and uses case-insensitive, diacritic-normalized display-name matching, including
fuzzy matches. Empty/whitespace query returns no matches. Date filters, CaseId,
unknown fields and unsupported search modes reject rather than being ignored;
legacy Lexical/DisplayName mode names remain accepted. Duplicate case aliases
such as `Type` plus `type` reject. Filters and erasure suppression apply before
paging and totals exclude erased entries.

The new Query DTOs have no payload paging members. When envelope Paging is
present, it alone governs: size defaults to 20, position to offset 0, maximum
size 100, and offsets must align with the effective size. A nonblank cursor
cannot combine with an offset. Cursors bind query type, tenant, user, filters
and size; changed scope rejects before reading. Response paging reports effective
size/offset, filtered total, hasMore and nextCursor. When envelope Paging is
absent, the legacy payload Page/PageSize behavior remains (page defaults to 1,
size to 20, maximum 100; nonpositive values reject).

# Hexalith.Memories

Hexalith Memory Module with syntactic and semantic search.

## Quick start

The guided quickstart gets you from a fresh clone to a first search result in under 30 minutes on a clean machine (NFR31 — approximate; see [docs/dev/quickstart.md](docs/dev/quickstart.md#manual-nfr31-walkthrough-cadence) for the manual walkthrough cadence). The current automated coverage focuses on the wizard itself against a warm fixture; the full clean-machine walkthrough remains a manual verification step.

### 1. Prerequisites (~30s to verify)

- [Docker Desktop](https://docs.docker.com/desktop/) (WSL2 on Windows; resource allocation on macOS)
- [.NET SDK 11.0.100](https://dotnet.microsoft.com/download/dotnet/11.0) and the [ASP.NET Core 10 runtime](https://dotnet.microsoft.com/download/dotnet/10.0) (including .NET 10) for the net10.0 applications and tests
- `git` with submodules support

If any of these fail, see [docs/dev/quickstart.md](docs/dev/quickstart.md) for OS-specific setup notes.

### 2. Clone and initialize submodules (~2 min cold)

```bash
git clone <repo-url> Hexalith.Memories
cd Hexalith.Memories
git submodule update --init
```

The root-declared submodules are checked out under `references/`: `references/Hexalith.Commons`, `references/Hexalith.EventStore`, `references/Hexalith.AI.Tools`, `references/Hexalith.Tenants`, `references/Hexalith.FrontComposer`, `references/Hexalith.Builds`, and `references/Hexalith.PolymorphicSerializations`.
The non-recursive `git submodule update --init` above initializes all of them; `references/Hexalith.FrontComposer` is required to build the `Hexalith.Memories.Web` component library. Initialize only these root-declared submodules; do not use `--recursive`.

### 3. Build the solution (~5 min first time, ~30s incremental)

```bash
dotnet build Hexalith.Memories.slnx
```

### 4. Boot this repository's test stack in a dedicated terminal (~1 min first time, ~20s subsequent)

```bash
dotnet run --project src/Hexalith.Memories.AppHost
```

On first AppHost run, a session-scoped OpenBao container starts and the AppHost generates OpenBao-backed `secretstores.hashicorp.vault` Dapr components automatically; there is no local `secrets.json` file. Wait for the Aspire dashboard to show the `memories` resource as Running.

`src/Hexalith.Memories.AppHost` serves only this repository's own tests, including this walkthrough. A run of it is never evidence that Memories runs in the Platform composition. To run or debug Memories as a module, use the Platform workspace (see [Run and debug from the Platform workspace](#run-and-debug-from-the-platform-workspace)).

### 5. Install the CLI (~1 min first time, ~10s subsequent)

```bash
dotnet pack src/Hexalith.Memories.Cli -c Release -o ./artifacts
dotnet tool install -g --add-source ./artifacts Hexalith.Memories.Cli
```

### 6. Run the guided quickstart (<1 min on a warm stack)

In a second terminal (while the AppHost continues running in the first):

```bash
memories quickstart
```

The wizard verifies prerequisites, prints the stack boot command, probes server health, provisions a sample tenant, ingests a sample document, and runs a validation search. On success you'll see `Quickstart ok in <N>s across 6 steps.`

**Total** (warm cache, approximate): ~10 min. Cold-start first-time: approximately 25-30 min (network + Docker image pulls; record manual walkthrough timings in [docs/dev/quickstart-walkthrough-log.md](docs/dev/quickstart-walkthrough-log.md)).

**If a step fails**, consult [docs/dev/quickstart.md](docs/dev/quickstart.md) for the per-step failure decision tree.

## Run and debug from the Platform workspace

Memories runs and debugs as a module from the [Hexalith.Platform](https://github.com/Hexalith/Hexalith.Platform) workspace, where this repository is the direct submodule `references/Hexalith.Memories`. Prerequisites:

- The Platform-pinned `hexalith-module` tool, restored with `dotnet tool restore` in the Platform root.
- Aspire CLI `13.6.1` exactly; the tool refuses any other version with `HXR015`.
- A running Docker engine.
- `HEXALITH_DAPR_HOME` set to an absolute, isolated Dapr home: Dapr CLI `1.18.0` at `tools/dapr` and runtime `1.18.2` at `.dapr/bin/{daprd,placement,scheduler}`. The Platform README shows how to prepare one from the official release assets.
- The Platform workspace's direct `references/Hexalith.Builds`, `references/Hexalith.EventStore`, `references/Hexalith.Tenants` and `references/Hexalith.Memories` checkouts, initialized without `--recursive`, with each `HEAD` matching its staged Platform gitlink. The tool reads all three declaration owners even though Memories does not run Tenants. After a local commit here, run `git add references/Hexalith.Memories` in the Platform root before starting a run.
- The local Aspire orchestration and dashboard packages at `13.6.1`: run `dotnet restore apphost.cs` from Platform once before the first `debug` run. Tool restore alone does not install these SDK packages. If NuGet uses a custom `globalPackagesFolder`, set `NUGET_PACKAGES` to that absolute folder for both restore and `debug`; otherwise the tool checks `~/.nuget/packages` and reports `HXR016` when packages are missing.

From the Platform root:

```bash
export HEXALITH_DAPR_HOME="$HOME/.hexalith/dapr/1.18.2"
dotnet tool run hexalith-module -- debug --manifest references/Hexalith.Memories/module/hexalith.module-manifest.v2.json
dotnet tool run hexalith-module -- down --manifest references/Hexalith.Memories/module/hexalith.module-manifest.v2.json
```

Pass the owner manifest under `references/`, never the Platform's copy in `src/Hexalith.Platform.Composition/Declarations/`. `debug` builds this checkout and the Platform workspace's `references/Hexalith.EventStore` in Debug and starts the declared selection, Memories and EventStore with no Tenants: the `memories`, `memories-access-telemetry-clock`, `memories-access-telemetry` and `eventstore` servers with their Dapr sidecars, plus Redis Stack (`memories-vectors`) and FalkorDB (`memories-graph`). It waits for each server's `/ready` endpoint and reports one `dotnet run` launcher process id per server. Each application is its launcher's child process:

```bash
ps --ppid <launcher-pid> -o pid,args
```

Attach to the child running the server's `bin/Debug/net10.0/<Assembly>` executable, for example with VS Code ("Attach to a .NET process"). Breakpoints in this checkout's sources bind. Stay attached until you finish, then stop only that run with `down`.

`debug` does not print the run id: it is the file name of the run state `<runId>.json` under `${XDG_DATA_HOME:-$HOME/.local/share}/hexalith-builds/g4-runs/` on Linux. Inspect the state files and select the one whose `projectProcessIds` contains the launcher id reported by this `debug` invocation. Confirm its `manifestHash` matches `sha256sum references/Hexalith.Memories/module/hexalith.module-manifest.v2.json` (ignoring hexadecimal letter case), then use its `runId`. File modification time alone cannot identify your run. When an earlier run used the same manifest, `down --manifest` refuses with `HXR024`; add `--run-id <runId>`. An explicit `--run-id` is not cross-checked against the manifest, so verify both fields before stopping it.

# Hexalith.ChatBot

Hexalith.ChatBot is the governed email-to-project orchestration module for the Hexalith platform. Epic 1 establishes the command spine, contract-first client, Aspire/DAPR topology, first governed UI command, and safety-floor test harnesses. Epic 2 adds Microsoft 365 mailbox intake, participant resolution, deterministic association scoring, S2 association review, decision/correction history, correction-propagation metadata, and duplicate/retry/failure status foundations. Epic 3 adds the S1 project-conversation projection, email/participant/attachment/decision/approval/failure/AI-outcome rendering, the "why this project" evidence panel, attachment capture and safety states, and an auditable AI-context package manifest for authorized files. Epic 4 adds governed AI action mediation: task-intent capture and review, deterministic AI-action risk classification, low-risk assistance routing, S3 approval records and decisions, metadata-only preview/inspection, M0 allowlisted approved execution, safe refusal cataloging, and corrected-context invalidation for stale AI proposals. Epic 5 adds service-client identities and scoped grants, the production CLI adapter, the governed MCP tool surface, and real UI/API + CLI + MCP differential-conformance verification over the shared command spine. Epic 6 adds governed outbound communication and inbound authenticity. Epic 7 adds tenant administration and governance policy. Epic 8 adds operational observability and runtime activation. Epic 9 adds tamper-evident audit, compliance investigation, and recovery validation. Epic 10 adds the governed chat surface and FrontComposer shell adoption. Epic 11 moves the Server host to `Hexalith.EventStore.DomainService`, migrates queries/projections/read models/cursors/telemetry/health to SDK contracts, and retires standalone ChatBot Aspire/ServiceDefaults packages. Epic 12 completed Fluent UI v5 component conformance remediation: the raw-control backlog and CSS primitive backlog are empty, and `ChatBotFluentConformanceTests` is the build-blocking guard. Epic 13 completed FrontComposer page-level layout-composition remediation: every routable page composes through `FcPageLayout` + `FcPageHeader` and Fluent layout/data components, the hand-rolled `.chatbot-*` page chrome and `<dl>` data dumps are gone, the sibling `ChatBotLayoutCompositionConformanceTests` guard's allowlists are empty, and the six surfaces are re-verified against the real rendered app.

## Aspire and DAPR

The retained AppHost is a local-development umbrella only. It wires ChatBot with EventStore, Tenants, Keycloak, and DAPR sidecars while reusable hosting behavior stays in the EventStore DomainService SDK.

The default AppHost launch profile selects `Development`, which loads the AppHost user secrets (`hexalith-chatbot`). Configure the [mailbox secret](#local-service-credentials) before starting; external Projects/Memories endpoints and tokens are optional overrides. Start it from the repository root with `aspire run`, or use `aspire start --non-interactive` for a detached agent session. The dashboard uses `https://localhost:17278`.

Runtime component names are intentional:

- `statestore` is the canonical EventStore actor/status/archive/checkpoint store.
- `chatbot-statestore` is ChatBot's derived read-model and coarse-idempotency store.
- `chatbot-workflow-statestore` is ChatBot's hosted Dapr Workflow state store.
- `chatbot-pubsub` is the Redis pub/sub component carrying governed events.

The local self-hosted Aspire topology loads `src/Hexalith.ChatBot.AppHost/DaprComponents/accesscontrol.local.yaml` because mTLS is disabled. Production must use the deny-by-default `accesscontrol.yaml` with mTLS/Sentry enabled.

Production ChatBot deployments must configure a shared DataProtection key ring with `ChatBot:DataProtection:KeyRingPath`, or explicitly set `ChatBot:DataProtection:SingleReplicaOnly=true`. The admission marker and query cursor key ring cannot be ephemeral for restart-surviving or multi-replica claims.

Epic 2 correction propagation now has hosted Dapr Workflow runtime binding for the live topology. `AddChatBotCorrectionPropagationWorkflow()` registers the workflow and activities, `Program.cs` enables it when `ChatBot:UseDaprWorkflowRuntime=true`, and the AppHost sets that flag for the ChatBot service. EventStore remains the lifecycle source of truth; Dapr Workflow coordinates the saga and must not be described as a replacement aggregate or sibling-context mutation path.

Epic 3 project conversation context is currently a ChatBot-owned read projection in `chatbot-statestore`, exposed through the contract spine and consumed by the S1 Blazor surface. Do not describe it as a `Hexalith.Conversations` adapter path unless that adapter is added in code.

Epic 4 AI mediation is currently implemented inside the ChatBot command spine. `DeterministicAiActionRiskClassifier` and `AiActionApprovalGate` are the registered gateway stages, `ExecuteLowRiskAIAssistance` uses the scoped context-package contract, and approved M0 execution is constrained by `ai-action-command-allowlist.m0` to `Project.AppendConversationMessage`. The current conversation writer is metadata-only; do not describe it as a durable sibling `Hexalith.Conversations` write until that binding exists in code.

Epic 5 CLI and MCP surfaces are implemented as thin adapters over `Hexalith.ChatBot.Client`. The CLI uses `System.CommandLine`, the MCP server uses `ModelContextProtocol`, and both submit typed commands through `IChatBotClient.SubmitAsync` with their surface origin. They must not be described as direct DAPR/EventStore/projection clients or as local authorization/governance layers.

The Epic 5 differential-conformance harness now drives the production CLI and MCP adapter translation paths plus the UI/API client seam. Do not describe current parity verification as only M0 CLI/MCP shims.

Epic 6 outbound and authenticity behavior is implemented inside the ChatBot command spine. `SenderAuthorityClassifier`, `OutboundDraftAuthorityEvaluator`, and `OutboundSendAuthorityEvaluator` own sender-authority decisions; outbound drafts are ChatBot-local records; outbound sends require the outbound approval commands and single-shot `outbound-send` idempotency before the outbound mailbox sender seam is reached. Inbound Microsoft 365 authenticity is provider passthrough only: ChatBot records selected SPF/DKIM/DMARC/composite-authentication/header metadata, delegated-sender posture, and external-sender strictness signals without re-verifying DNS or trusting raw headers over provider identity.

Epic 7 tenant administration and governance run inside the ChatBot command spine. `AdminAuthorityEvaluator` owns the bounded admin-scope model (`AdminScope`/`AdminRole`), and the shared `GovernedOperationAggregate` drives the two-person submit→approve pattern for policy changes and the disable/quarantine/rate-limit control floor. The control-floor enforcement seams differ by subject (worker intake for mailbox sources, the service-client grant validator for service clients and AI actors, the top of `ParticipantAuthorizationStage` for command capabilities, and the send seam in `AcceptedCommandDispatcher` for outbound channels). The command allowlist is always widened last, after validation/authorization/audit, and Epic 7 admin operations keep audit metadata-only. Most Epic 7 admin surfaces (queues, notification routing, escalation, throttling, backlog, rubber-stamp) ride the existing generic command-submission transport and add no new public HTTP paths; only the admin/policy and control-floor command DTOs were added to the OpenAPI component schemas.

Epic 7 control-state and rate-limit enforcement has been activated for the server runtime seams by Epic 8.7a/8.7b. `CommandGatewayServiceCollectionExtensions` now registers projection-backed service-client, AI-actor, command-capability, and outbound-channel control/rate-limit providers, and the architecture tests guard against reintroducing `AlwaysActive…` or `AlwaysUnlimited…` providers on that path. The mailbox worker path still has only the projection-backed provider foundation and static stubs; do not describe mailbox-source runtime enforcement as fully live until a hosted worker path consumes `GovernedControlStateView`.

Epic 8 observability emission is always-on, and the deferred evaluator set now has one owned periodic runtime. The `Hexalith.ChatBot` meter and its instruments are registered by the Server host alongside `AddEventStoreDomainTelemetry("chatbot")`. `Program.cs` enables `AddChatBotPeriodicEnforcementHostedService()` when `ChatBot:UsePeriodicEnforcementRuntime=true`, and the AppHost sets that flag. The periodic coordinator drives escalation, notification throttling, reviewer backlog, rubber-stamp, operational alerts, weekly runbook sampling, audit completeness publication, audit-projection-lag publication, and control-state freshness heartbeats. Remaining caveats are explicit: the S8 UI still assembles a fail-safe all-`Unknown` placeholder until a dashboard read endpoint is wired, and `IAuditProjectionLagSource` is swapped to `CheckpointBackedAuditProjectionLagSource` only to publish measured checkpoints when available; the default checkpoint source still returns no readings because governed-operation projection positions are not exposed yet. Do not describe audit lag as live-measured until that checkpoint feed is backed by real positions.

Epic 9 follows the same build-the-logic / defer-selected-live-drivers pattern. The WORM audit chain append rides the existing commit seam, and Story 9.2 audit completeness now has a periodic publication path through the Epic 8.7b runtime. The nightly chain verifier, replay-isolation and derived-store-isolation probes, correction-reindex SLO-deadline sweep, and continuity-drill / projection-rebuild / scoped-outage validation harnesses (9.11–9.13) remain coordinator/release-gate seams without live fault-injection / rebuild / Hexalith.Memories vector drivers (`IContinuityDrillScenarioRunner`, `IProjectionRebuildDriver`, `IScopedOutageInjectionDriver`, and the live `IDerivedStore` binding are deferred or in-memory by default). The NFR56–59 recovery targets (RPO ≤ 15 min, RTO ≤ 4 hr) remain A10 [ASSUMPTION] values not yet recalibrated against a live drill. Unlike Epics 7 and 8, Epic 9 added new public HTTP paths: Story 9.3 wired `POST /api/v1/compliance/audit/search` and `GET /api/v1/compliance/audit/{auditRecordRef}` (the S9 investigation surface) over the existing OpenAPI compliance schemas, widening the audit `filterKey` set with `message-id` and `surface`. Those paths and filter keys are now reflected in `src/Hexalith.ChatBot.Contracts/openapi/hexalith.chatbot.v1.yaml`; the client still carries the hand-written `ComplianceAuditTransport`, so a contract-first client regeneration remains the follow-up (Epic 9 retrospective action item #6).

Epic 10 adds the governed Project Workspace chat surface on the same command spine, plus FrontComposer Shell ownership for the UI. User messages use metadata-only `RecordProjectConversationMessage`; ask-AI requests route through the Epic 4 proposal path; Stop/Cancel uses `CancelAiResponseGeneration` through `IChatBotClient.SubmitAsync` and CommandGateway. AI response progress is exposed through typed project-conversation read models (`AiResponseProgress`) and nudged by a ChatBot-owned metadata-only SignalR hub at `/hubs/chatbot/project-conversation-changes`. The hub is enabled by `ChatBot:ProjectionChangeNotifications:Enabled=true`; the AppHost sets this for local runs. SignalR carries only a tenant-scoped "project conversation changed" signal, never response text, raw provider chunks, prompts, hidden policy detail, or exception content; the UI always re-queries typed server state before rendering progress or terminal Stop/Cancel results. Epic 10 also surfaced a UX-DR1/UX-DR2 component-conformance gap: Shell adoption landed correctly, but interior UI components still used raw controls and a custom `chatbot.tokens.css` layer. Epic 12 closed that gap by migrating ChatBot UI controls to Fluent v5 components, retiring the custom CSS primitive layer to Fluent-backed semantic aliases plus layout/accessibility hooks, and proving the empty guard through UI, E2E, conformance, CLI, MCP, and architecture lanes. Epic 13 then closed the page-level composition gap Epics 10 and 12 left open: pages had still hand-rolled chrome with `.chatbot-page-header`/`.chatbot-page`/`.chatbot-command-bar` CSS that overlapped the FrontComposer shell top bar, boxed content in a 1px border, and rendered primary data as monospace `<dl>` dumps. Each page was re-composed through `FcPageLayout` + `FcPageHeader` with Fluent layout/data components (`FluentDataGrid`, `FluentStack`, `FluentCard`, `FluentAccordion`), mirroring `Hexalith.Tenants.UI`; the retired layout CSS and the empty allowlists are enforced by the sibling `ChatBotLayoutCompositionConformanceTests` guard. ### Local service credentials

The AppHost renders the Keycloak realm on every run — including ordinary local development unrelated to Story 12.15's live-recovery lane — and fails closed if `ChatBot:LiveRecoveryValidation:MailboxClientSecret` is not configured. ```

helper. Each run enrolls separate `chatbot-projects-owner` and `chatbot-memories-owner` Keycloak clients with secret

and `platform-owner-operation.`: Projects receives `hexalith-eventstore` / `projects:read`; Memories receives
`hexalith-memories-server` / `memories:derived-store`. These REST identities do not gain SDK workload caller access.

and EventStore's tenant-scoped endpoints authorize on that claim alone. Projects and Memories derive the tenant from `tenant_id`.
The operation scopes identify the adapter's token requests and cache entries; they do not add receiver authorization.
Projects requires the `eventstore:permission=projects:read` mapper at its claim-transformation authorization gate.
Memories natively grants authenticated tenant membership, including access to its supported

continues to enforce its own permissions, tenant provisioning and project access gates.

fallback. Foreign destinations, redirects, insecure non-loopback HTTP and cross-tenant Project-context requests are denied.

and [production identity contract](references/Hexalith.Projects/docs/runbooks/projects-production-identity-contract.md),

### Local-development seed-credential policy

Every client, user, and secret the AppHost renders into `KeycloakRealms/hexalith-realm.json` is a **local-development seed**, not a provisioned credential. The AppHost is `IsPublishable=false` and is never a production hosting path, so:

- **The service-client grants deliberately share one expiry.** They are seeds re-minted on every non-persistent run, not credentials with independent lifecycles, so staggering them would model a rotation story this host does not own. Configure the expiry with `ChatBotServiceGrants:ExpiresAtUtc`, or its lifetime with `ChatBotServiceGrants:LifetimeDays` (default 90 days).
- **The pre-expiry gate is the guardrail.** `PrepareKeycloakRealmImport` refuses to start the topology when the grant expiry is less than `ChatBotServiceGrants:MinimumRemainingDays` (default 30) in the future — the failure mode a stale checked-in realm actually produces. The expected placeholder count is derived from the realm's own `chatbot-service-client-grant-expiry` protocol mappers, so adding a realm client cannot silently opt that client out of the gate, and a mapper that lost its placeholder fails naming the offending client id.
- **`KeycloakPersistent=true` weakens that gate.** A reused Keycloak container does not re-import the realm, so the expiry validated at startup may not be the one Keycloak is serving. The AppHost warns on stderr in this mode; remove the Keycloak container (`docker rm -f`) to force a re-import after changing the realm or the configured expiry.
- **The recovery validator is a static test fixture.** The committed `recovery-validator` user and `recovery-validator-pass` password belong only to the local sandbox realm. `RecoveryValidatorIdentity` supplies the same values to recovery token requests; they are intentionally not rotated per run. The topology contract tests verify that the user stays in the reserved recovery tenant, separate from both control tenants, and that the token request matches the realm. This documented fixture residual is not production credential or rotation evidence.
- **Production provisioning and rotation live outside the AppHost**, in deployment configuration. Do not add provisioning, rotation, or a deployment manifest to `Hexalith.ChatBot.AppHost`.
